title: Athlete’s foot: treating a fungal infection and reducing recurrence
intro: Athlete’s foot is a fungal infection of the skin of the feet, not a condition limited to athletes. It can cause itching, scaling and cracks, often between the toes, but may also affect the soles or sides. Other skin conditions can look similar. Effective care combines an appropriate diagnosis and antifungal treatment with attention to moisture and opportunities for the fungus to spread.

sections.heading: Recognise the symptoms without assuming every rash is fungal
paragraphs: The skin may peel, look whitish and damp between toes, or become dry and scaly elsewhere. Small blisters or soreness are possible. Colour changes may be less obvious on darker skin. Eczema, contact allergy and other problems can resemble fungal infection. If the appearance is unusual, symptoms keep returning or treatment fails, ask for assessment rather than repeatedly switching products. A clinician may examine the skin or take a sample when the diagnosis is uncertain.

sections.heading: Choose treatment that fits the person and the site
paragraphs: Antifungal creams, sprays or other preparations are available, but suitability and instructions differ. A pharmacist or clinician can advise, especially for children, pregnancy, other illnesses or medicines. Follow the recommended course rather than stopping only because itching eases or applying more to speed results. Do not use someone else's treatment. Nail changes may need separate assessment because treating the surrounding skin does not automatically treat a fungal nail infection.

sections.heading: Avoid treatments that can hide the problem
paragraphs: A steroid cream alone can mask or worsen some fungal infections, even if redness or itching briefly improves. Do not borrow a steroid or use a combination product without appropriate advice. Harsh chemicals, bleach and aggressive scraping can damage skin and are not a safe shortcut. Tell the professional which products you have already tried and whether the area became more painful or irritated. This helps distinguish persistent infection from irritation or an incorrect diagnosis.

sections.heading: Make moisture control and hygiene practical
paragraphs: Dry feet carefully after washing, including between the toes, and change damp socks. Allow footwear to dry and choose options that suit your activity without keeping feet constantly moist. Do not share footwear or towels, and use suitable footwear in communal changing areas. These measures help limit exposure and recurrence but do not replace necessary treatment. Discuss recurrent problems if work boots, sweating or limited access to washing make the usual advice difficult to follow.

sections.heading: Know when to seek medical help early
paragraphs: Get advice if symptoms spread, persist despite the recommended course, involve nails or repeatedly recur. Diabetes, poor circulation, reduced sensation or weakened immunity call for particular care with foot problems. A hot, increasingly painful or swollen foot, spreading inflammation, a wound or fever needs prompt assessment rather than being treated as ordinary athlete’s foot. Protect broken skin and avoid cutting or digging at it. Ask what follow-up is needed if the diagnosis remains unclear.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: reviewing repeated treatment failure
examples.text: Someone has itchy peeling skin despite several pharmacy products. They bring the product names and describe how they used them at an appointment. They ask whether the diagnosis needs confirmation instead of assuming a stronger product or a steroid cream will solve it.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: recognising a different level of risk
examples.text: A person with diabetes notices a painful crack and new warmth and swelling of the foot. They seek prompt medical assessment rather than waiting for an antifungal cream to work. They explain their diabetes and the recent change in symptoms.

questions: Does this look like a fungal infection, or would a skin sample or another diagnosis be useful?
Which treatment and course are appropriate for my skin, health conditions and medicines?
What changes suggest infection or another complication, and how can I reduce recurrence realistically?
